## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta* ("The Shorter Discourse on the Lion’s Roar", MN 11) is the eleventh discourse of the Majjhimanikāya and the opening sutta of the *Sīhanādavagga* [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Delivered at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove, the sutta records the Buddha's bold assertion that genuine recluses representing the four stages of awakening are found solely within his dispensation [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. He explains that while other contemplative traditions may recognize and renounce attachment to sensual pleasures, views, and rules or observances, they fail to transcend grasping at a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*) [Anālayo 2010; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The discourse also discusses the eradication of clinging and the attainment of non-return when clinging remains with residue (*sa-upādisese*) [Anālayo 2010].

In commentarial history, the *Mahāvaṁsa-ṭīkā* notes that the ancient Sinhalese commentary to the *Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta* preserved historical narratives regarding Janasāna and the mother of King Asoka, details that were not retained in Buddhaghosa's Pali commentary [Walpola Rahula 1956]. Modern English translations include those by Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Bhikkhu Sujato, I.B. Horner, and Suddhāso Bhikkhu [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995].

Full parallels are preserved in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 103), the *Ekottarika-āgama* (EĀ 27.2), and the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (AN 4.241) [SuttaCentral]. In comparative studies, Anālayo points out that where the Pali version specifies grasping at a "doctrine of self" (*attavādupādāna*), the Chinese parallels and a Sanskrit fragment parallel speak directly of clinging to "a self" (*ātmopādāna*) [Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2017; Bingenheimer 2018]. DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-language alignments with the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* and *Ekottarika-āgama*, while also identifying alignments with the Sanskrit *Pravrajyāvastu* and *Dharmaskandha* [DharmaNexus]. Across the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records extensive text reuse across 104 texts, sharing major textual sequences with the *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), and the *Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta* (MN 38) [DharmaNexus].
